The Sooty-capped Hermit (Phaethornis augusti) emerges from its calcareous egg at a remarkably early stage of development. Field data indicate that incubation at a stable temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] produces hatching after approximately 20 days [ab = approximately 20 days], a duration consistent with other medium-sized trochilids that incubate under tightly regulated thermal conditions. Neonates emerge at a wet weight of just 0.60 grams [Ww0 = 0.60 grams], a modest initial mass that reflects the altricial state of the newly hatched chick. This low birth mass places the species at the lower end of the range for hermit hummingbirds and necessitates an intensive period of parental provisioning, during which the nestling must more than double its mass before reaching independence. The rapid growth trajectory that follows is energetically demanding, and the nest-depended chick relies entirely on the female for thermoregulation and food delivery during the first critical days post-hatching. The delicate nature of these pin-feathered chicks underscores the selective pressures acting on the early post-hatching period in Phaethornis augusti.

Nestling growth proceeds swiftly, and the brood attains a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.65 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.65 grams] before the onset of rapid mass accumulation. Under the thermal conditions typical of the adult's active metabolic state (38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]), fledging — marked by the achievement of sustained flight and feather maturation — occurs at 24 days since birth [tx = 24 days since birth]. This relatively short nestling period is comparable to that of other Neotropical hermits, reflecting a life-history strategy that prioritizes rapid development in response to high predation pressure within the understory. By this stage, the developing chick has undergone extensive organogenesis and feather growth, transitioning from a downy, brooded nestling to a flight-capable juvenile capable of leaving the nest. The 38.1 °C body temperature maintained during this period facilitates efficient metabolic processing of the protein-rich diet delivered by the female, which is composed primarily of nectar and small arthropods.

Sexual maturation in this species occurs considerably later than fledging, a pattern typical of long-lived tropical birds that invest heavily in survival. Puberty is attained at 72 days since birth [tp = 72 days since birth] under the same 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C] thermal regime, a threshold that coincides with the completion of skeletal growth and the onset of gonadal maturation in captive-reared individuals. Field observations corroborate this timing, with subadult birds first displaying territorial behavior and the characteristic lekking vocalizations associated with reproductive activation at approximately two and a half months of age. This relatively early puberty among hummingbirds may be linked to the species' ability to exploit a predictable nectar resource, allowing young individuals to accumulate sufficient condition for reproductive effort without an extended pre-reproductive juvenile period. The attainment of reproductive maturity marks a significant physiological transition, involving increased circulating steroid hormones and the development of the specialized gape morphology used during nectar extraction.

The timing of first reproduction follows a markedly different schedule from the attainment of sexual maturity. The first brood is initiated at 365 days since birth [tR = 365 days since birth], a full year after hatching, when maintained at 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This delay reflects the intense energetic demands of reproduction in a small endotherm, as females must first secure a high-quality territory and accumulate sufficient lipid stores to sustain the extended incubation and provisioning periods. Reproductive output is limited, with females producing a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch] and typically completing just over two clutches per year [F_R_i = two clutches per year], a low rate that is characteristic of hermits. The combination of a year-long delay to first breeding and a modest annual fecundity suggests a bet-hedging strategy in a relatively stable tropical environment, where adult survival is prioritized over high immediate reproductive output.

Lifespan estimates for Phaethornis augusti, derived from mark-recapture studies and extrapolated from related species such as Archilochus alexandri, suggest a maximum longevity of 10 years [am = 10 years] at a body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This is a notably long lifespan for a bird of its size and aligns with the general life-history syndrome of tropical hummingbirds, which trade high annual survival against low fecundity. The ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown adults is 5.5 grams [Wwi = 5.5 grams], a value that places the Sooty-capped Hermit among the larger members of the Phaethornithinae subfamily. This adult body mass is consistent with its foraging ecology as a long-billed trapline forager, requiring sufficient mass to sustain daily energy expenditures across large home ranges. The combination of slow development, delayed reproduction, and extended lifespan underscores the species' position on the slow end of the life-history continuum for trochilids.
